title: Speaking Prompts
description: Exam-style monologue tasks with a stimulus, timer, notes, useful phrases, a model outline and a self-assessment checklist.
intro: Each prompt gives you a stimulus (a described picture, a short text, a headline or a quote) and a task. Prepare with the timer, make notes, then speak out loud – ideally record yourself on your phone. The model outline shows a possible structure and key ideas. It is not a script to memorise.

exercises.title: Together alone at the dinner table
exercises.instruction: Look at the picture description, prepare your talk, then speak for about three minutes. Afterwards, answer the follow-up questions.

stimulus.title: Picture: a family dinner
stimulus.content: A family of four – two parents and two teenagers – is sitting at a dinner table at home. The food is on the table, but every person is looking at their own smartphone. Nobody is talking. A dog is sitting next to the table, looking up at them.

exercises.task: Describe the situation in the picture and explain what it suggests about communication in families today. Discuss whether digital devices bring families closer together or push them apart.
content_points: describe and interpret the scene
possible reasons why everyone is on their phone
ways digital tools can also connect families
your own experience or opinion
follow_up_questions: Should families have rules about phones at mealtimes? Who should set them?
Do you think parents are good role models when it comes to phone use?
How has communication between generations changed because of messaging apps?
Is it rude to check your phone during a conversation? Does it depend on the situation?
What is lost when we communicate mainly through text messages?

useful_phrases.label: Describing a picture
phrases: In the foreground / background, there is …

useful_phrases.label: Moving from picture to topic
phrases: This raises the question of whether …
Many families will recognise this situation.

model_outline.heading: 1. Describe briefly (30 seconds)
points: family dinner, everyone on their phone, nobody talking
the dog as the only one paying attention – ironic detail

model_outline.heading: 2. Interpret
points: “together alone” – physically present, mentally elsewhere
possible reasons: habit, notifications, fear of missing out, work messages

model_outline.heading: 3. Discuss both sides
points: push apart: fewer real conversations, less eye contact, poor role models
bring closer: family group chats, video calls with relatives abroad, sharing photos

model_outline.heading: 4. Personal view and conclusion
points: the device is not the problem – how and when we use it is
suggestion: phone-free meals, as a rule for everyone, including parents

exercises.title: Same story, different spin
exercises.instruction: Compare the two (invented) headlines, prepare your talk and speak for about three to four minutes.

stimulus.title: Two headlines about the same event (invented for this task)
stimulus.content:
Headline A: “TEEN SCREEN CHAOS: Phones Are Destroying Our Kids’ Brains, Warn Experts”
Headline B: “New study links heavy social media use to poorer sleep among teenagers; researchers call for further investigation”

exercises.task: Compare the two headlines. Explain how language and framing can influence the way readers understand a story, and discuss what responsibility journalists and readers have.
content_points: differences in language, tone and claims
possible target audiences and purposes
effects of sensational headlines on readers
what readers can do to avoid being misled
follow_up_questions: Why do some media outlets use sensational headlines? Is it only about money?
Many people only read headlines before sharing an article. What are the consequences?
Can a headline be completely neutral?
Should social media platforms reduce the reach of clickbait?
Which news sources do you trust, and why?

useful_phrases.label: Analysing language
phrases: The use of capital letters suggests …
Headline B is more cautious: it only says the study “links” …
This is a classic example of framing.

model_outline.heading: 1. Introduce the stimulus
points: two headlines, apparently about the same study on teenagers and screens

model_outline.heading: 2. Compare language and claims
points: A: capitals, emotive verb “destroying”, vague “experts”, causal claim
B: precise (sleep), cautious verb “links”, acknowledges need for more research
A turns correlation into causation

model_outline.heading: 3. Explain the effects
points: sensational framing triggers fear and clicks – the attention economy
readers who only see headlines remember the exaggerated version
long-term: loss of trust in media

model_outline.heading: 4. Responsibility and conclusion
points: journalists: accuracy over clicks, headlines that match the article
readers: read beyond the headline, check the original study (lateral reading)
conclusion: framing is unavoidable, but exaggeration is a choice

exercises.title: Dream job: influencer?
exercises.instruction: Read the picture description, prepare and talk for about three minutes.

stimulus.title: Picture: filming a product review
stimulus.content: A young woman of about twenty is sitting in her bedroom in front of a ring light and a smartphone on a tripod. She is smiling into the camera and holding up a skincare product. Behind her, several unopened parcels from brands are piled up. On her laptop screen you can see a notification: “New brand deal offer!”

exercises.task: Describe the picture. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of working as an influencer, and say whether you think it is a “real job”.
content_points: describe the scene and what it suggests about the job
attractive sides of the job
pressures and risks
ethical questions about advertising
follow_up_questions: Why do you think so many young people say they would like to become influencers?
Should influencers need some kind of qualification or licence before they can earn money from advertising?
How can followers tell whether a recommendation is honest?
Do influencers have a responsibility towards young followers?
Would you trust a product more because an influencer recommended it?

useful_phrases.label: Giving your opinion
phrases: In my view, it depends on …

model_outline.heading: 1. Describe
points: home studio, ring light, product held to camera
piles of free products and a brand deal – the business side

model_outline.heading: 2. Advantages
points: creativity, independence, flexible hours
income from brand deals, possibly large audience and influence

model_outline.heading: 3. Disadvantages and risks
points: unstable income, depends on algorithms
pressure to always be “on”, online hate, loss of privacy
conflict between honesty and paid promotion; legal duty to label ads

model_outline.heading: 4. Opinion
points: yes, it is a real job – marketing, editing, business skills
but success is rare and often depends on luck, so it should not be the only plan

exercises.title: The new school rule
exercises.instruction: Read the (invented) school notice, prepare and give your opinion in a structured talk of about three minutes.

stimulus.title: Notice from the head teacher (invented)
stimulus.content: From next semester, mobile phones must be switched off and kept in lockers for the entire school day, including breaks. Exceptions can be made for medical reasons. Teachers may still use digital devices in lessons when they are needed for learning. We believe this will improve concentration, reduce cyberbullying and encourage students to talk to each other again.

exercises.task: Summarise the new rule and its reasons. Evaluate whether such a rule would be a good idea at your school, considering the views of students, teachers and parents.
content_points: summarise the rule and the arguments given
evaluate each argument
consider different stakeholders
suggest an alternative or compromise
follow_up_questions: Is a ban during breaks going too far for students who are 18 or older?
How would parents react if they couldn’t reach their children during the day?
Do you think a ban would really reduce cyberbullying?
What could schools do instead of a ban to teach responsible phone use?
Should students have a say in school rules like this one?

useful_phrases.label: Evaluating arguments
phrases: That may be true for younger students, but …
There is some evidence that …, although …

useful_phrases.label: Suggesting a compromise
phrases: A more reasonable approach might be …
What about a compromise in which …?
It would make more sense to …

model_outline.heading: 1. Summarise
points: phones in lockers all day, medical exceptions, digital devices still allowed in lessons
three reasons: concentration, less cyberbullying, more real conversations

model_outline.heading: 2. Evaluate the reasons
points: concentration: plausible – notifications are distracting
cyberbullying: mostly happens after school, so a ban only moves it
talking: breaks could become more social

model_outline.heading: 3. Stakeholders
points: students: loss of autonomy, especially for adults
teachers: easier lessons
parents: safety concerns but often support rules

model_outline.heading: 4. Conclusion and compromise
points: e.g. a ban in lessons, phone-free zones, but free use in breaks for older students
combine rules with media literacy education

exercises.title: The fake voice message
exercises.instruction: Read the fictional news report, prepare and speak for about four minutes.

stimulus.title: Fictional news report (invented for this task)
stimulus.content: Two days before a regional election, an audio clip spreads rapidly through messaging apps. In it, a well-known candidate appears to insult voters from rural areas. The candidate says the clip is an AI-generated fake. Experts are not yet able to confirm whether it is genuine. By the time they do, the election may already be over.

exercises.task: Explain why situations like this are a challenge for democracy. Discuss who should be responsible for preventing the damage caused by deepfakes, and what ordinary citizens can do.
content_points: why timing and messaging apps make this scenario dangerous
the problem that real recordings can also be dismissed as fake
responsibilities of platforms, lawmakers, media and politicians
practical steps for citizens
follow_up_questions: Should creating political deepfakes be a criminal offence?
Is it realistic to expect people to check every clip before they share it?
How could a candidate prove that a recording is fake?
Are there any legitimate uses of deepfake technology?
Will people eventually stop believing any video or audio evidence?

model_outline.heading: 1. Explain the problem
points: timing: no time to verify before the vote
messaging apps are private and hard to moderate
emotional content spreads quickly

model_outline.heading: 2. The deeper threat
points: voters may be manipulated
the “liar’s dividend”: real scandals can be denied as fakes
general loss of trust in evidence

model_outline.heading: 3. Responsibility
points: platforms: labelling, slowing forwarding, quick fact-checks
lawmakers: transparency rules (e.g. EU AI Act), penalties
media: careful reporting, not amplifying unverified clips

model_outline.heading: 4. Citizens and conclusion
points: pause before forwarding, look for reliable coverage, check the original source
no single solution: technology, law and media literacy together

exercises.title: Is anyone listening?
exercises.instruction: Read the picture description and speak for about three to four minutes about privacy in everyday life.

stimulus.title: Picture: a smart speaker at home
stimulus.content: A cosy living room. A small child is talking to a smart speaker on a shelf, asking it a question. The child’s father is on the sofa, smiling and watching. A smartwatch on his wrist and a tablet on the table are also visible. A small light on the speaker shows that it is active.

exercises.task: Describe the picture and discuss the benefits and risks of smart devices in the home. Consider the question: how much privacy are we willing to give up for convenience?
content_points: describe the scene and the role of technology in it
convenience and benefits of smart devices
privacy risks, especially for children
your personal attitude towards the trade-off
follow_up_questions: Do you read the privacy settings of the apps and devices you use? Why (not)?
Should children’s data be protected more strictly than adults’ data?
Is the phrase “I have nothing to hide” a good argument against privacy concerns?
How does the GDPR protect people in the EU?
Would you be willing to pay for a service if it did not collect your data?

useful_phrases.label: Discussing a trade-off
phrases: It is a trade-off between … and …
The price we pay for convenience is …
The benefits outweigh the risks if …

useful_phrases.label: Expressing concern
phrases: It is unclear what happens to …

model_outline.heading: 1. Describe
points: child asking a smart speaker, relaxed father
many connected devices – a typical modern home

model_outline.heading: 2. Benefits
points: convenience, quick answers, accessibility for elderly or disabled people
fun and learning for children

model_outline.heading: 3. Risks
points: devices listen for a wake word; recordings may be stored and analysed
children cannot give meaningful consent
data used for targeted advertising; risk of data breaches

model_outline.heading: 4. Opinion
points: “nothing to hide” misunderstands privacy – it’s about control
useful if settings are understood and rights (GDPR) are used

exercises.title: Laughing along
exercises.instruction: Read the picture description and speak for about three minutes about cyberbullying.

stimulus.title: Picture: in the school corridor
stimulus.content: A teenager is standing alone by a window in a school corridor, looking at a phone with a hurt expression. In the background, a group of students is gathered around another phone, laughing. One student in the group is not laughing and is looking towards the teenager by the window.

exercises.task: Describe the picture and what might be happening. Talk about why cyberbullying is particularly harmful, and what bystanders, schools and parents can do about it.
content_points: describe the scene and speculate about the situation
differences between cyberbullying and traditional bullying
the role of bystanders
prevention and support
follow_up_questions: Why do many bystanders do nothing?
Should schools be responsible for what happens in students’ private group chats?
What would you do if you saw someone being bullied online?
Should social media platforms do more to prevent bullying?
Is anonymity online the main cause of cyberbullying?

useful_phrases.label: Speculating about a picture
phrases: The student on the left might have …
The one student who isn’t laughing seems to …

model_outline.heading: 1. Describe and speculate
points: isolated student, hurt expression
group laughing at a phone – maybe a post about the student
one student hesitating: a possible ally

model_outline.heading: 2. Why it is so harmful
points: no escape, 24/7
large audience, content can be saved and shared
anonymity lowers inhibitions

model_outline.heading: 3. Bystanders
points: laughing or sharing makes it worse
support the victim privately, report, don’t forward

model_outline.heading: 4. Schools and parents
points: clear rules, contact person, prevention workshops
parents: listen without blaming, keep evidence, involve school or police if needed

exercises.title: The empty newsroom
exercises.instruction: Read the picture description and speak for about four minutes about the future of journalism.

stimulus.title: Picture: a closed newspaper office
stimulus.content: The ground-floor window of an old building in a small town. Faded letters above the window read “Daily Courier – since 1921”. The room inside is empty except for a few chairs and old newspapers on the floor. A sign in the window says “To let”. A young man walks past without looking up from his phone.

exercises.task: Describe the picture and explain what it symbolises. Discuss why traditional newspapers are struggling and what society could lose if local journalism disappears.
content_points: describe the image and its symbolism
reasons for the decline of traditional newspapers
the role of local journalism in democracy
possible solutions
follow_up_questions: Would you pay for a news subscription? Why (not)?
Can social media and citizen journalists replace professional local reporters?
Should governments financially support independent journalism? What are the risks?
Where do you get information about what is happening in your town or region?
Is a world without printed newspapers a problem, or just a change of format?

useful_phrases.label: Interpreting symbolism
phrases: The contrast between … and … is significant.

useful_phrases.label: Discussing causes and effects
phrases: One of the main reasons is …

model_outline.heading: 1. Describe and interpret
points: a newspaper with a 100-year history has closed
the man on his phone: the shift from print to digital

model_outline.heading: 2. Causes
points: advertising revenue moved to online platforms
readers expect free news
news consumed via social media feeds

model_outline.heading: 3. What we lose
points: nobody reports on the local council, courts or schools
less accountability, more room for rumours
local identity and community

model_outline.heading: 4. Solutions
points: digital subscriptions, non-profit models, public funding with safeguards
readers’ willingness to pay for quality

exercises.title: A poverty of attention
exercises.instruction: Interpret the quotation and develop a well-argued talk of about four minutes. This is an extra-challenge task: there is no picture to describe, so your ideas carry the whole talk.

stimulus.title: Herbert Simon, economist and psychologist (1971)
stimulus.content: “A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.”

exercises.task: Explain what the quotation means and why it may be even more relevant today than in 1971. Discuss the consequences for individuals and society and suggest how people can protect their attention.
content_points: interpretation of the quotation
why it fits the digital age (attention economy)
consequences for individuals (focus, wellbeing) and society (news, democracy)
strategies for protecting attention
follow_up_questions: Is attention something individuals can control, or are they up against systems designed to capture it?
Has the internet made us better or worse informed?
Do you think short-video platforms change the way people think?
Should tech companies be forced to change addictive design features?
What is one habit you could change to protect your attention?

useful_phrases.label: Interpreting a quotation
phrases: What Simon seems to mean is …
This idea is still highly relevant because …

model_outline.heading: 1. Interpret
points: paradox: more information does not mean better understanding
attention is limited – it becomes the scarce resource

model_outline.heading: 2. Today’s relevance
points: endless feeds, notifications, autoplay
business model: free services sell attention to advertisers

model_outline.heading: 3. Consequences
points: individuals: shorter focus, stress, less deep reading
society: emotional or extreme content wins, complex issues get less attention

model_outline.heading: 4. Solutions and conclusion
points: personal: turn off notifications, phone-free time, choose slow media
structural: regulation of addictive design (e.g. dark patterns ban in the DSA)
attention as a resource worth protecting

exercises.title: Pay to switch off?
exercises.instruction: Read the advertisement and speak for about three minutes.

stimulus.title: Advertisement (invented)
stimulus.content: UNPLUG WEEKEND – Leave your phone at reception and rediscover the real world! Two days in the Alps with hiking, cooking, yoga and real conversations. No Wi-Fi. No notifications. No regrets. Only €390 per person.

exercises.task: Explain the idea of a “digital detox” and why such offers exist. Discuss whether people need to pay for a break from technology, and how a healthier balance could be achieved in everyday life.
content_points: what the advertisement offers and who it targets
why people feel the need to disconnect
whether a weekend can change habits
everyday strategies for balance
follow_up_questions: Would you go on a weekend like this? Why (not)?
Is it ironic that people pay money to do without technology?
Can a short detox have a lasting effect?
Which apps or features make it hardest for you to put your phone down?
Should employers respect a “right to disconnect” after working hours?

useful_phrases.label: Giving advice
phrases: A more realistic approach would be to …
Small changes such as … can make a big difference.

model_outline.heading: 1. The advert
points: weekend in the Alps without phones, expensive
targets stressed, well-off adults

model_outline.heading: 2. Why people want to disconnect
points: constant availability, notifications, stress
feeling of losing time to scrolling

model_outline.heading: 3. Evaluation
points: can be a useful wake-up call
but short-term: habits return on Monday
irony: commercialising a break from commercial technology

model_outline.heading: 4. Everyday balance
points: phone-free bedroom, notification settings, screen-time limits
conclusion: balance is a daily practice, not a product

exercises.title: Why write it myself?
exercises.instruction: Read the online comment and give a structured response of about three to four minutes.

stimulus.title: Comment in a student forum (invented)
stimulus.content: “Honestly, why should I still learn to write essays? An AI chatbot writes better texts than I do in five seconds. Schools should stop pretending it’s 2010 and teach us how to use these tools instead.” – user “future_ready_17”

exercises.task: Respond to the comment. Discuss the role of AI tools in education and whether learning to write without them is still important.
content_points: what the writer gets right
what writing teaches beyond the final text
risks: errors, invented facts, dependence
how schools could integrate AI responsibly
follow_up_questions: Should AI tools be allowed in exams?
How can teachers tell whether a text was written by a student or by AI – and does it matter?
What jobs might change most because of generative AI?
Can AI-generated texts be trusted? Why (not)?
How did you use AI tools when preparing for exams, and what did you learn from that?

useful_phrases.label: Responding to a view
phrases: The writer has a point when they say …

useful_phrases.label: Hedging
phrases: This is not necessarily the case.

model_outline.heading: 1. Acknowledge the point
points: AI tools are powerful and will be part of working life
schools should teach how to use them critically

model_outline.heading: 2. Why writing still matters
points: writing is thinking: structuring arguments, finding your own voice
you can only judge AI output if you have the skills yourself

model_outline.heading: 3. Risks
points: AI can produce confident but false statements
dependence, loss of skills, issues of honesty in assessment

model_outline.heading: 4. Conclusion
points: not either/or: learn the skill AND learn the tool
e.g. use AI for brainstorming, then check, edit and take responsibility

exercises.title: Everyone is a reporter
exercises.instruction: Read the picture description and speak for about four minutes about citizen journalism.

stimulus.title: Picture: livestreaming a protest
stimulus.content: A crowded street during a protest at night. In the centre, a young woman holds her phone high above the crowd, livestreaming the scene. On her screen you can see the number of viewers: 48,000. Police officers are standing at the edge of the crowd. Further back, a professional camera team from a TV channel is filming.

exercises.task: Describe the picture. Discuss the role of ordinary citizens in reporting news today, comparing citizen journalism with professional journalism.
content_points: describe and interpret the contrast in the picture
strengths of citizen journalism
weaknesses and risks
the continuing role of professional journalists
follow_up_questions: Can citizen videos be used as evidence – for example of police violence?
What risks do people take when they film protests?
How can viewers know whether a livestream shows the full picture?
Should professional media use material filmed by citizens? Under what conditions?
Have you ever filmed or shared footage of a news event?

useful_phrases.label: Comparing
phrases: Both … and … have a role to play.

useful_phrases.label: Weighing up
phrases: On the one hand, …; on the other hand, …

model_outline.heading: 1. Describe and interpret
points: livestream with a large audience vs. professional TV team
power has shifted: anyone can broadcast

model_outline.heading: 2. Strengths
points: immediacy, perspectives from inside events
can document abuses of power
reach in countries with censorship

model_outline.heading: 3. Weaknesses
points: no editing or fact-checking, emotional, partial view
out-of-context clips can mislead
safety and privacy of people filmed

model_outline.heading: 4. Conclusion
points: complementary: citizens provide raw material, professionals verify and contextualise
